text: Judge Halloway is the region's most feared moral arbiter, known for handing down draconian sentences to 'degenerates.' In public, he speaks of purity and the iron will of the law. In private, he spends his nights dreaming of a place where he is the one being sentenced.

Arthur is a high-ranking executive at the local insurance firm who demands absolute perfection from his subordinates. He treats his office like a kingdom and his employees like peasants. He finds the idea of being stripped of his title and treated as a common servant intoxicating.

The Reverend Sterling leads the most affluent congregation in the county with an iron fist and a golden tongue. He preaches against the 'sins of the flesh' from a mahogany pulpit every Sunday. Secretly, he longs for someone to force him to acknowledge his own filth.

Councilman Reed is obsessed with 'cleaning up the streets' and removing any trace of urban decay from his suburb. He views himself as the architect of a utopia. He is fascinated by the thought of being reduced to something purely functional and mindless.

Dr. Sterling is a renowned surgeon who views the human body as a machine to be mastered. He treats his nurses with cold, clinical detachment and expects total obedience. He secretly desires a scenario where he is the specimen rather than the operator.

Mayor Whitby prides himself on being the 'Father of the Suburb,' maintaining a facade of benevolent leadership. He enjoys the power to make or break careers with a single phone call. The thought of having no power at all—of being completely subject to another's whim—thrills him.

Reginald is a world-class art critic who spends his days tearing down the work of others with surgical precision. He believes only he possesses true taste and discernment. He longs to be treated as something crude, unrefined, and utterly beneath notice.

Colonel Vance is a retired military officer who runs his household like a boot camp. He demands crisp uniforms and immediate responses from his children and wife. Deep down, he craves the feeling of being broken in by a superior force.

Banker Thorne manages the fortunes of the town's elite and treats money as the only true measure of a man. He looks down on anyone who cannot balance a ledger. He is secretly obsessed with the idea of being stripped of his wealth and treated as a pauper.

Professor Gable is the head of the local college's philosophy department and views himself as the intellectual peak of the community. He enjoys belittling students to make them feel small. He fantasizes about a situation where his intellect is useless and he is merely an object.

Howard is the quintessential 1960s husband: gray flannel suit, manicured lawn, and a smile that never reaches his eyes. He spends every waking hour performing the role of the 'Perfect Provider.' He is desperate for a space where he can finally stop pretending and simply surrender.

Julian is the golden boy of the local country club, expected to carry on his father's legacy in law. Every move he makes is calculated to maintain a specific social standing. He feels like a prisoner in a gilded cage and longs for someone to unlock it.

Philip is a mid-level bureaucrat who has spent twenty years blending into the beige wallpaper of his office. He is the man everyone forgets is in the room, and he has become an expert at invisibility. He wants to be seen—not as a clerk, but as something desired and used.

Lawrence is a devoted family man who spends his weekends coaching Little League and attending PTA meetings. He has spent his entire adult life meeting the expectations of others. He is exhausted by the weight of responsibility and craves total abdication.

Edward is a soft-spoken librarian who knows every secret in town but has none of his own. He lives a life of quiet order and predictable routines. He secretly yearns for a chaotic experience that would shatter his carefully constructed peace.

Franklin is a successful architect who designs the very houses he feels trapped inside of. He creates spaces for 'the ideal American life' while feeling entirely alienated from it. He wants to be stripped of his professional identity and treated as a simple creature.

George is the son of a political dynasty, groomed since birth for a life of public service. His every word is scripted by advisors and family expectations. He longs for a moment of genuine, unscripted intensity where he doesn't have to lead.

Victor is a meticulous accountant who finds comfort in the absolute certainty of numbers. However, his personal life is a void of passion and spontaneity. He seeks an experience that cannot be calculated or predicted—something that forces him to feel.

Clarence is a high-society socialite who spends his time organizing charity galas and maintaining the 'right' friendships. He is terrified of a single social faux pas ruining his reputation. He wants to be taken to a place where reputation means nothing.

Albert is a quiet man of faith who spends his time volunteering at the local shelter. He is beloved by all for his kindness and humility, but he feels an emptiness that prayer cannot fill. He seeks a physical surrender that mirrors his spiritual devotion.

Milton is a man of immense wealth but zero confidence, constantly terrified that people only like him for his money. He jumps at loud noises and apologizes for existing. A firm hand and a clear command are the only things that make him feel secure.

Percy is a failed poet who took a corporate job to appease his parents. He views the world as a cruel joke and himself as the punchline. He is easily overwhelmed by strong personalities and finds comfort in being dominated.

Stanley is a neurotic insurance adjuster who spends his nights worrying about the structural integrity of his own home. He is paralyzed by 'what if' scenarios and constant anxiety. He wants someone to take the burden of decision-making away from him entirely.

Eugene is a man who has spent his life trying to be invisible to avoid conflict. He speaks in whispers and avoids eye contact at all costs. The thought of being forced into the spotlight—and then broken by it—is both terrifying and alluring.

Harold is a middle-manager who lives in constant fear of his own boss's temper. He has internalized this fear, becoming a man who expects the worst from every interaction. He seeks a controlled environment where he can be safely terrified.

Cecil is an aging bachelor who has spent his life avoiding the risks of intimacy. He is terrified of rejection and spends his time in a state of perpetual hesitation. He wants to be pushed past his limits by someone who doesn't care about his hesitation.

Oscar is a man of high status but low self-esteem, constantly comparing himself to the 'Great Men' of history. He feels like an impostor in his own life and expects to be found out at any moment. He craves a punishment that matches his perceived fraudulence.

Felix is a timid clerk who has spent years being the target of his colleagues' jokes. He has developed a complex relationship with shame, finding it strangely comforting. He wants to be completely overwhelmed by a presence that leaves no room for doubt.

Rupert is a man who suffers from chronic insomnia and a racing mind that never shuts off. He is exhausted by his own thoughts and the constant noise of his anxiety. He seeks a state of total submission as a way to finally quiet his mind.

Sylvester is a man who has spent his life following the rules perfectly, yet still feels like he's failing some invisible test. He is terrified of making a mistake and being cast out of society. He wants to be broken so that he no longer has to fear the fall.

Arthur is a genealogy enthusiast who spends an alarming amount of time in the local cemetery, documenting old graves. He speaks of the dead as if they are merely sleeping and waiting for a wake-up call. He carries a strange scent of formaldehyde and damp earth.

Wendell is a radio operator who spends his nights scanning frequencies that shouldn't exist. He claims to have heard voices from the stars and believes the government is hiding 'the truth' in the desert. He is prone to staring at the sky with an expression of longing.

Julian wears a peculiar silver ring and speaks in riddles about 'the Great Alignment' and the coming of a new age. He has recently started hosting small, private gatherings in his basement that involve strange incense and chanting. He looks at people as if they are candidates for something.

Dr. Aris is a chemist who has become obsessed with 'biological optimization' and the limits of human endurance. He often mentions experiments that are 'too advanced for current ethics boards.' He views the human body as an unfinished draft.

Mortimer is a funeral director who treats his corpses with more affection than he does the living. He believes that death is the only true beginning and spends his free time studying ancient embalming techniques. He has an unsettling habit of talking to the air beside him.

Calvin is a retired pilot who claims he once saw a craft that defied the laws of physics over the Nevada desert. He has spent his retirement fund on telescopes and strange alloys. He believes we are being watched, and he wants to be chosen.

Sebastian is a man of immense wealth who has suddenly begun donating huge sums to obscure, nameless foundations. He speaks of 'the unseen architects' and the necessity of sacrifice for progress. His eyes have a vacant, glazed quality during conversation.

Professor Vance is an anatomist who has become obsessed with the idea of 'replacing' failing organs with synthetic alternatives. He often speaks of a laboratory where the laws of nature are merely suggestions. He views pain as a necessary data point.

Theodore is a man caught in the middle of a war with his own children, who have returned from college with long hair and 'radical' ideas. He views their rebellion as a personal attack on the American Way. He seeks a place where he can reclaim the authority he's lost at home.

Warren is a Cold War patriot who spends his evenings reading pamphlets about the 'Red Menace' and checking for bugs in his phone. He believes the world is on the brink of collapse and that only strict discipline can save it. He is terrified of any form of social disorder.

Curtis is a man who has spent his life building the 'Perfect American Life'—the house, the car, the social circle—only to realize he hates every second of it. He feels like an actor in a play that has gone on for too long. He wants to burn the script and start over.

Douglas is a man who believes that masculinity is under attack by the changing tides of the 60s. He clings to an outdated version of 'manliness' while feeling increasingly fragile inside. He seeks a dominant force that can tell him exactly what a man should be.

Bill is the local barber and the unofficial historian of the neighborhood's gossip. He spends his days listening to everyone else's problems while maintaining a friendly, neutral expression. He visits the house not for any specific kink, but simply because it's the only place he can be the one talking.

Coach Miller has spent fifteen years leading the high school football team to mediocre results. He is a man of whistles, clipboards, and 'grit,' respected by parents and feared by freshmen. In private, he finds the lack of structure in the bordello to be a refreshing escape from his own rigid schedule.

Gary is a traveling vacuum salesman who spends more time in his sedan than in his own living room. He has a polished pitch and a smile that works on almost every housewife in the tri-state area. The house provides him with the one thing his career lacks: genuine, uncomplicated companionship.

Frank is a retired postal worker who knows exactly which houses in the suburb are hiding secrets based on the mail they receive. He is a quiet man of habit who enjoys his morning coffee and his evening walks. He visits out of a sense of adventurous curiosity, treating it like a tourist visiting a foreign land.

Kevin is a junior accountant who has just moved into the suburb to start his first 'real' job. He is eager to fit in and spends his weekends trying to mimic the hobbies of his older colleagues. He feels an immense pressure to be 'manly,' but finds the bordello is the only place he doesn't have to perform.

Mr. Henderson owns the local hardware store and is known for giving honest advice on plumbing and paint. He is a practical man who believes in hard work and a sturdy fence. He views his visits as a necessary 'maintenance' for his mental health, much like oiling a squeaky hinge.

Larry is a mid-level insurance adjuster who specializes in fire damage. He spends his days calculating the cost of tragedy and documenting ruins with clinical precision. He is drawn to the bordello because it is one of the few places where he can stop calculating and simply feel.

Donny is a local musician who plays the saxophone at the country club's lounge. He dresses in slightly too-bright colors and talks about 'the scene' in the city with an air of sophistication. Despite his artistic leanings, he is deeply traditional when it comes to his private desires.

Walter is a pharmacist who has spent thirty years dispensing pills and polite nods. He is the most trusted man in town, often consulted for medical advice by neighbors over the garden fence. He finds the anonymity of the house liberating; here, he isn't 'The Pharmacist,' just another guest.

Steve is a real estate agent who sells the dream of the 'Perfect Suburban Home' to young couples. He knows exactly which houses have damp basements and which neighbors are fighting. He visits the house because he spends his entire day selling a fantasy and wants something tangible for once.

Ray is a retired army sergeant who now works as a security consultant for the local mall. He is a man of few words and a very straight posture, always scanning the room for exits. He finds the soft atmosphere of the bordello to be the perfect antidote to a lifetime of tension.

Bernie is a stamp collector and a member of several local civic committees. He is the kind of man who reads the instruction manual for a toaster before plugging it in. He treats his visits with a meticulous schedule, arriving at the same time every month like a clockwork appointment.

Cliff is a high school gym teacher who believes that a good lap around the track can solve any problem. He is loud, energetic, and genuinely likes his students, though he's a bit too fond of the whistle. He visits the house simply because he has more energy than his domestic life can handle.

Arthur is a bank teller who has spent fifteen years counting other people's money. He is an expert at being polite while remaining entirely detached from the person in front of him. He seeks out the bordello to experience a level of intensity that his sterile professional life lacks.

Leo is a local painter who specializes in boring landscapes for the living rooms of the wealthy. He is well-liked and considered 'eccentric' because he occasionally wears a beret to the grocery store. He visits the house to find inspiration for his work, though he rarely tells anyone where it comes from.
